name: Stenodontes exsertus
intro: The Puerto Rican giant longhorn is a larger, redder relative of Stenodontes chevrolati. The adults I have seen have long, curved mandibles with a smooth inner edge. The species occurs on Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. My breeding notes come from Puerto Rican stock, and keeping the laying medium almost dry made a real difference to the eggs.

facts.title: Laying setup
facts.text: About 2 inches (5 cm) of nearly dry sawdust, with bark on top

sections.title: Eggs
sections.text: I put about 2 inches (5 cm) of sawdust in the breeding container and lay pieces of bark on the surface. The sawdust I use is very nearly bone dry. In a damp laying bed the eggs have molded and rotted, and young larvae have also rotted. For that reason I avoid using moist flake soil or white-rotten wood as the laying bed for my Puerto Rican stock. The bark gives the adult cover without having to wet the whole bed.

sections.title: Larvae
sections.text:
I can rear the larvae in the same sort of sawdust. By February 23, 2026, I had rehoused 36 of them and was still working through the group. That is a count of the larvae I moved that day. In late March the young larvae I had available measured about 7–10 mm. They are small enough at that stage that it is worth taking the sawdust apart carefully.
I have also used kinshi, wood substrate colonized by a fungus, for the feeding larvae. Most of my S. exsertus were doing well on an oyster-mushroom batch when I checked them in November 2026. I had put Callipogon proletarius larvae on that same batch and lost every one of them. The contrast is worth keeping in mind when choosing a fungus for longhorn larvae. A substrate that supports a feeding larva also has a different job from the dry bed I give a laying female.
Lee et al. (2021, fig. 3) photographed early Callipogon relictus feeding in individual dishes. Their photographs show the scale of a newly hatched prionine beside a ruler.

sections.title: Adults
sections.text: I have reared unidentified longhorn larvae from fallen logs in Puerto Rico. The ones I took from those logs turned out to be Callipogon when they matured. Finding a large larva in a downed log was therefore a poor way for me to identify S. exsertus. A published host record for S. exsertus names Zanthoxylum, the prickly ashes.
